Case Vignette: "Ngozi"

Ngozi is a 35-year-old woman who presents for therapy at the urging of her partner, David. She describes herself as "tired of being afraid in my own skin." She is a private tutor for high school students, specializing in mathematics and science. She has been with David for four years, and they live together in a quiet suburb.

The trauma occurred eighteen months ago, on a Thursday evening in late autumn. Ngozi had just finished a tutoring session at a student's home in a neighboring town. She was walking to her car in the dimly lit parking lot of a small strip mall when a man approached from behind. He pressed something sharp into her back-she never saw a weapon, but she felt the point-and forced her into the back seat of her own car. He drove her to a secluded area behind an abandoned warehouse. There, he raped her. He did not speak during the assault, except to tell her, "Don't look at me." He left her in the car, on the floor of the back seat, with her keys on the dashboard. She lay there for what felt like hours before she could move.

In the weeks that followed, Ngozi did not tell anyone. She showered repeatedly, scrubbing her skin until it was raw. She threw away the clothes she had been wearing. She stopped driving at night. She began canceling tutoring sessions that required her to travel to unfamiliar neighborhoods, telling her clients she had a scheduling conflict. She did not sleep in the same bed as David for three months, claiming she was "too hot" or "restless." When he asked what was wrong, she said she was stressed about work.

The first time she told anyone was six months later, during a routine gynecological exam. The doctor's touch on her inner thigh triggered a flashback so vivid that she screamed. The doctor sat with her for an hour and helped her call a crisis line. Ngozi spoke to a counselor twice, then stopped. "I didn't want to be a victim," she says now, her voice flat.

Presently, Ngozi's life has narrowed. She still tutors, but only students who come to her home. She has arranged her schedule so that she never finishes a session after 4:00 PM, because she cannot tolerate the fading light of late afternoon. She avoids the strip mall where it happened, taking a 20-minute detour even to go to the grocery store. She has not driven her own car since the assault; David drives her everywhere, or she takes public transportation. She says the car "feels like a coffin."

Her sleep is fragmented. She wakes three to four times a night, often from nightmares in which she is trapped in a small, dark space with a faceless presence. She has learned to sleep with the bedroom door open and a lamp on in the hallway. She cannot tolerate being touched from behind. David has learned to approach her only when she can see him coming, and he always announces his presence before entering a room. She feels guilty about this, but she cannot control the jolt of terror that shoots through her when she is surprised.

At work, she is patient and effective with her students, but she has become hypervigilant about the doorbell. Every ring makes her heart pound. She checks the locks on her windows three times before bed. She has stopped listening to music with lyrics, because certain songs-she cannot predict which-trigger a sense of dread.

She says she feels "disconnected" from her own life, as though she is watching herself move through the world from a great distance. She has not felt pleasure in over a year. She loves David, but she often feels numb when he holds her. She says she is "here, but not here."

Ngozi is a thin woman with a careful, measured way of speaking. She holds her hands folded tightly in her lap during sessions, and she avoids eye contact when discussing the assault. She is articulate and intelligent, but her voice drops to a whisper when she talks about the parking lot. She has come to therapy because she is afraid she is "disappearing," and because David told her gently that he cannot watch her shrink any further. She wants to feel like herself again, but she is not sure who that person is anymore.
